Because there are ways to order the prime factors, and ways to place dividers, this gives us an initial ways to arrange divisors.

However, through this method, we overcount cases where is combined with another factor. For example, the arrangement can be written as or . Precisely, we double count any case with as a factor, triple count any case with , quadruple count any case with , etc.

Now, consider all cases where must be grouped with at least one . This can be expressed in the same "line" format as , where dividers can again be placed to group divisors. In this case, there are ways to order divisors, and ways to place dividers, so we have an possible sequences for this case. Notice that in this format, we double count cases where is a factor, we triple count cases where is a factor, etc. Precisely, for any case counted times in the first step, it is counted times in this step. Thus, if we subtract, we count each case exactly once.

Solution 12 (The simplest solution)[edit]

is factored as . There are ways of placing (or not placing) a '' between five ’s. These placements can be grouped into pairs. We create these by pairing each permutation with its corresponding permutation, made by replacing each '' of the one permutation with a blank space, and each blank space with a ''. So, in each pair of possible arrangements, the total number of ''s is .

We now have almost represented as , except we need to incorporate the 3 factor. We can either multiply with one of the powers of in between the adjacent ''s, or place in the spaces between/beyond the powers (so that we have a single in the product).

We first take the case where we multiply on of the powers of by . We see that since each placement of powers of has one more power than it does ''s, and since we have ''s in each pair of placements, there must be powers of in between adjacent ''s. We can multiply our factor of by any of the powers in the pair, each different power that we multiply by giving us unique solution. Thus, we have unique solutions that come from each pair when we multiply by .

Secondly, we can include on its own, in between its own set of ''. We can put the anywhere in between the powers of or at either end of the permutation. There are places between the powers of in any pair (equal to the number of ''s) and places at the end of the equations, giving us more solutions.

We have ways of decomposing from one pair, and we have pairs. The answer is then .
